newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Key Australian senator to be charged with fraud.
newsitem.headline: Key Australian senator to be charged with fraud.

text.p: Australian authorities said on Tuesday that a key independent senator would be charged with fraud -- throwing into doubt the government's ability to push contentious legislation through parliament.
Attorney-General Daryl Williams said senator Mal Colston would be summonsed on fraud charges over travel allowance claims and the use of frequent flyer points.
He added that a former government senator would also be charged with fraud.
Colston's vote has been crucial to the conservative Liberal-National government's success in pushing legislation through the hostile upper house of parliament, the Senate.
A fraud conviction would force him out of parliament.

Colston defected from the Labor opposition last year to sit as an independent and was then elected as Senate deputy president with government backing. He would have to be replaced by a Labor member if forced out of parliament.

"Senator Colston is being summonsed on charges ... in relation to allegations of defrauding the Commonwealth (government) on matters associated with travel allowance and use of frequent flyer points," Williams said in a brief statement.
He gave no further details because the matter would be dealt with in court.

Colston's replacement by a Labor member would give Labor and other leftist minority parties a total of 38 votes in the 76-seat chamber -- enough to tie a vote on government bills and therefore block legislation.
Colston, who has denied any wrongdoing, repaid almost A$7,000 (US$5,100) in misclaimed travel allowances earlier this year after blaming the incident on sloppy book-keeping by a member of his staff.

Prime Minister John Howard called for a police investigation after the Colston staffer retracted a previous statement accepting blame for the overclaimed expenses. Colston resigned as Senate deputy president in May.

Williams announced that former Liberal senator Noel Crichton-Browne would also be charged with fraud -- the third current or recently-retired member of the 16-month-old government to face such charges.
The allegations against Crichton-Browne relate to abuse of spouse entitlements -- perks allowing politicians to take their spouse or partner with them on trips.
Crichton-Browne was forced to quit in 1996 after the Liberal Party withdrew support for him in an internal power row.

Another former Liberal senator, Bob Woods, and a sitting National Party lower house MP, Michael Cobb, have already apeared in court on fraud charges relating to abuse of parliamentary benefits. All three men deny any wrongdoing.
